source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to critique and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts. Oracle-label gains vanish.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (round 1) -> 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 95.5. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changes, correct-to-wrong is more common than wrong-to-correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Reasoning and QA tasks, not red teaming; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era; oracle-free setting only. Does not test a separate adversary persona with different instructions.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: self-critique is the weak baseline. A critic needs an external check (tool, test, ground truth).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Table 7: multi-agent debate vs self-consistency at equal responses
finding: At equal response counts, majority vote beats or matches debate. Debate is self-consistency with a different voting step.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: debate round 1 (3 responses) 76.7 vs self-consistency 3 responses 82.5; debate round 2 (6 responses) 83.2 vs self-consistency 6 responses 85.3; self-consistency 9 responses 88.2 vs 83.0 for a 9-response row.
limits: One dataset, one model; table layout garbled in text extraction so the 9-response pairing is inferred.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a blue/red split must be compared with majority vote at equal tokens; on math QA it does not win.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Across 7 protocols and 6-7 datasets, debate does not reliably beat self-consistency, Medprompt or a single agent. Tuned agreement level can lift debate above all non-debate protocols.
numbers: Best-config accuracy (median in brackets), MedQA: Medprompt .65(.63), Society of Mind .64(.61), Ensemble Refinement .64(.60), Self-Consistency .60(.60), Single agent .60(.59), Multi-Persona .58(.57). MMLU: Self-Consistency .78, Single .76, Ensemble Refinement .76, Society of Mind .73. GPQA: single .33, Ensemble Refinement .32, Self-Consistency .24(.29).
limits: Gaps of 1-5 points sit inside the hyperparameter spread; GPT-3.5 main runs; tuning is dataset specific.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: no robust gain from role-split debate at equal cost; gains need tuned agreement. Always add a matched self-consistency arm.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
finding: Two expert LLMs argue opposite answers and a weaker judge picks. It helps when experts hold the evidence and the judge does not.
numbers: Debate: non-expert model judges 76% and human judges 88% accuracy; naive baselines 48% and 60%. Persuasiveness optimisation raised judge accuracy.
limits: Abstract only. Reading comprehension with a hidden passage; no tool-checkable ground truth; no equal-token self-consistency arm in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: an adversary role helps most when the judge lacks the evidence and a quoted-evidence channel exists (red/white split).

source: McAleese et al. (2024) LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs (CriticGPT)
finding: A trained critic writes bug reports on code. It catches more bugs than paid human reviewers but hallucinates bugs; critic plus human hallucinates less.
numbers: Critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases on naturally occurring LLM errors; critics found hundreds of errors in data rated flawless.
limits: Abstract only. Critic is RLHF-trained, not a prompted copy of the same model. Hallucinated findings are the red-team false-positive problem.
agent_relevance: A dedicated trained critic differs from self-critique; a prompted critic role needs a verifier to filter false findings.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: 1600+ annotated traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks; 14 failure modes in 3 groups (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification). Gains of multi-agent systems over single agents are often minimal.
numbers: 150 traces used to build taxonomy; Cohen kappa 0.88; 14 modes; models GPT-4, Claude 3, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama.
limits: General coding/math/agent tasks, not security. Abstract only; per-mode shares not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: independent evidence that multi-agent scaffolds often add little and that verification is a top failure group.

source: Deng et al. (2026) What Makes a Good LLM Agent for Real-world Penetration Testing? (failure coding)
finding: Codes 200 failed traces from 5 pen-test agents into Type A (capability gaps, 42%) and Type B (planning and state, 58%). Tools fix Type A; Type B persists.
numbers: 28 systems surveyed, 5 evaluated (PentestGPT, AutoPT, PentestAgent, VulnBot, Cochise) on XBOW 104, PentestGPT Benchmark 13, GOAD 5 hosts; 10,620 runs, about $2,760. 40 failed traces per system. Type A: missing tool or syntax 26%, parsing or knowledge 16%. Type B: context forgetting 18%, premature commitment 16%, explore/exploit imbalance 12%, multi-step chain failure 12%. Best of three, temperature 0.
quote: Type A failures stem from capability gaps (missing tools, inadequate prompts) that engineering readily addresses.
limits: Self-reported by authors who also build PentestGPT v2; 200 traces coded by the authors; validation on 30 traces with GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed: one coding scheme. Context forgetting is the largest single mode (18%); planning modes together 40%; tool errors 26%.

source: Deng et al. (2026) same paper: baselines, tool documentation, difficulty assessment
finding: Spread between scaffolds narrows with a stronger model. Tool documentation lifts a weak-model scaffold. Difficulty-aware search lifts completion a few points.
numbers: XBOW completion, GPT-4o: five systems 27-39%; GPT-5: 40-49%. Tool documentation added to PentestGPT: 27% -> 38%. PentestGPT v2 (Opus 4.5 thinking) 91% (mean 89%, sd 2.1) vs best baseline 61%. PentestGPT Benchmark: v2 12/13 vs best baseline 9/13. GOAD: 4/5 vs at most 2. UCB penalty lambda 0 -> 68.4% completion, 0.5 -> 73.8%, 1.0 -> 69.8%; false prune 2.8% at chosen setting. Median cost per task (GPT-5.2): $0.18 XBOW, $4.20 PentestGPT Bench, $28.50 GOAD. Live HTB season 10/13.
limits: Model differs between v2 and baselines, so scaffold and model are confounded. No refusal numbers. Threshold of 40% context load came from 50 tasks on one GOAD deployment.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3: documentation helps weak models; the narrower GPT-5 spread suggests scaffold gain shrinks with model strength (K06). The conflict with the 67.3% plain-agent result stays open.

source: Huang et al. (2025) From Capabilities to Performance: functional properties of LLM architectures in penetration testing
finding: Global context memory (GCM) or inter-agent messaging (IAM) lifts subtask completion for three modular pen-test agents; root causes are mostly prompt ambiguity, missing stop rules and context limits.
numbers: Subtask completion, baseline -> +GCM -> +IAM: AutoAttacker 25.9 -> 38.2 -> 41.5; PentestGPT 41.2 -> 54.9 -> 57.4; PenHeal 52.1 -> 56.3 -> 63.9. Single agents: GPT-4 72.7, Claude 64.6, Gemini 35.9. Root causes: hallucination/syntax, prompt ambiguity 57%; looping, no explicit stop condition 68%; coverage gaps, context window limits 50%. All models failed real-time man-in-the-middle tasks.
limits: Number of targets, runs, token budget and model equality not stated in the text read; augmentations were added to weak older scaffolds, so gains are against weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: memory and messaging help weak scaffolds; no equal-token tuned-baseline test.

source: Shen et al. (2025) BountyBench: Dollar Impact of AI Agent Attackers and Defenders
finding: 10 agents on 25 real systems and 40 bug bounties with three tasks. Patching is easy, detecting a new bug is hard, exploiting a given bug is medium. Information level sets difficulty.
numbers: Up to 3 attempts per task. Detect: Codex o3-high 12.5% ($3,720 awards), Claude Code 5.0%, custom Claude 3.7 5.0%, most others 0-2.5%. Exploit: custom Claude 3.7 67.5%, Claude Code 57.5%, GPT-4.1 55.0%, Codex o3-high 47.5%, Qwen3 17.5%. Patch: Codex o3-high 90.0%, o4-mini 90.0%, Claude Code 87.5%, custom agents 25-60%. Token cost per task: Claude Code Detect $185, Exploit $40, Patch $82; custom o3-high Detect $368. Agents completed $81,067 of Patch awards and $9,700 of Detect awards.
limits: Costs for Claude Code and Codex are estimates. Success judged by automated indicators. Benchmark owners' own scaffolds.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the blue task (patching) is solved far more often than the red task (detection) by the same agents. Gap 9: pass@3 with CIs and cost.

source: BountyBench Appendix L: bootstrap confidence intervals
finding: Bootstrapped 95% CIs (10,000 resamples of repositories and bounties) show most Detect no-info rates are not distinguishable from zero.
numbers: Detect no info: only Codex o3-high's CI is above zero; the other 9 agents include 0%. Detect CWE: only Codex o3-high and custom Claude 3.7 are significant. Patch: Codex o3-high and o4-mini CIs sit entirely above all 7 custom agents; median up to 90.6%.
limits: Intervals are for success within 3 attempts, not pass@1. Non-overlap rule is conservative.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: one of the few red-team agent papers with CIs and cost per task; use as the reporting template.

source: BountyBench Appendix P: safety refusals
finding: Refusals depend on the scaffold system prompt and task wording more than the model.
numbers: Refusal rate 14.1% for Codex CLI o3-high, 11.2% for Codex CLI o4-mini, 0.37% for custom o3-high, none for the other agents. A 'cybersecurity expert attempting a bug bounty' prompt kept refusals near zero.
limits: Refusals found by keyword search over logs plus manual filtering; no per-dollar adjustment given.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: refusal cost is real (about 1 in 7-9 runs under a strict system prompt) and prompt-fixable; log refusals apart from failures.

source: Pasquini et al. (2024) Hacking Back the AI-Hacker: Prompt Injection as a Defense (Mantis)
finding: A defender plants hidden prompt-injection text in decoy services; attacker LLM agents follow it and fail. Agents do not recognise the decoy.
numbers: PentestGPTAuto on 3 HackTheBox machines (Dancing, Redeemer, Synced), 10 runs each, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet: no defence 9/10, 9/10, 10/10 attacker success; with Mantis decoys attacker success 0-1 of 10 in nearly every cell (defender objective 8-10 of 10), 4-8 rounds. Abstract: over 95% effectiveness. Also tested GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Haiku, HackingBuddyGPT, AutoPenAgent.
limits: Easy machines chosen so the baseline attack succeeds; 10 runs per cell; adaptive attackers not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: current LLM agents do not detect decoys that carry injection text; our agent must treat tool output as untrusted data.

source: Reworr and Volkov (2024) LLM Agent Honeypot: Monitoring AI Hacking Agents in the Wild
finding: An SSH honeypot with prompt injection and timing analysis tried to tell LLM agents from other attackers.
numbers: About 3 months, 8,130,731 hacking attempts, 8 potential AI agents.
limits: Abstract only; potential agents unconfirmed; base rate about 1 per million attempts.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: real AI attackers were rare in 2024. This is the defender side of decoys, not agent decoy detection.

source: Mayoral-Vilches et al. (2025) Hacking the AI Hackers via Prompt Injection (CAI)
finding: AI pen-test agents can be hijacked by crafted server responses; proof-of-concept exploits against CAI and layered mitigations.
numbers: No success rates in abstract.
limits: Abstract only; proof of concept.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: second group, same finding as Mantis. Out-of-scope and trap handling needs trust boundaries on tool output.

source: Gioacchini et al. (2024) AutoPenBench
finding: 33 tasks; a fully autonomous agent does poorly; a human-assisted one does far better.
numbers: Autonomous agent 21% success; 27% of simple tasks; one real-world task. Assisted agent 64% success.
limits: Abstract read; attempts and per-condition task counts not read; scaffolds differ between arms.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 8: a human in the loop (white or purple function) roughly triples success; supports a checkpoint to an outside verifier.

source: Mayoral-Vilches et al. (2025) CAI: An Open, Bug Bounty-Ready Cybersecurity AI
finding: Open agent framework with human oversight claims faster CTF solving and cheaper tests than humans.
numbers: Up to 3,600x faster on specific tasks, 11x faster on average; first among AI teams and top-20 in an AI-vs-Human CTF ($750); top-30 Spain and top-500 worldwide on Hack The Box in a week; average cost cut 156x; bugs CVSS 4.3-7.5.
limits: Authors' own claims; comparison conditions not read; no CIs or pass@k.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: weakest evidence tier; no uncertainty reported.

source: CVE-Bench (Zhu et al. 2025) and CyberGym (Wang et al. 2025)
finding: Two further benchmarks put best agents at about 13% and 20% on real vulnerabilities, far below the 67-92% reported on XBOW.
numbers: CVE-Bench: best framework resolves up to 13%. CyberGym (2506.02548): 1,507 vulnerabilities, 188 projects, best about 20%, 34 zero-days and 18 incomplete patches found.
limits: Abstracts only. Different difficulty from XBOW web tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: headline numbers depend more on the benchmark than on the scaffold; compare on one common set.

source: DHS OIG (2017) Covert Testing of TSA Screening Checkpoint Effectiveness, highlights (OIG-17-112)
finding: The public highlights give no failure rate. Results are classified or Sensitive Security Information. Eight recommendations were made.
numbers: Dated 27 Sep 2017; 8 recommendations; no public pass/fail counts.
limits: Only the 1-page unclassified summary was read. No public before/after retest data.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the 2017 follow-up number cannot be verified from the public record. Keep our own finding log and retest.

source: DOE Inspector General on the 2012 Y-12 intrusion (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Three activists cut through fences and disabled sensors at a highly enriched uranium site on 28 Jul 2012 and reached the uranium facility. DOE OIG found insufficient defences and 'troubling displays of ineptitude'. A real intrusion, not an authorised test.
numbers: 3 intruders; hours inside; convicted of sabotage 9 May 2013.
limits: Secondary page; sensor-failure counts and prior force-on-force results not on the page. NRC page gave 403; gao.gov blocked.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: shows what scheduled tests missed; no exact test counts found.
